title: Cicero: Addressing Algorithmic and Architectural Bottlenecks in Neural Rendering by Radiance Warping and Memory Optimizations
problem: Neural Radiance Fields execute extremely slowly on mobile GPUs (0.8 FPS on mobile Volta) due to both algorithmic bottlenecks (excessive computation, irregular DRAM accesses) and architectural inefficiencies (SRAM bank conflicts) that prevent adoption in VR/AR systems.
motivation: Neural rendering via NeRF offers a compelling alternative to traditional rendering but current performance limitations prevent deployment in resource-constrained mobile devices.
method: Cicero optimizes neural rendering on mobile GPUs by fixing two fundamental problems through software alone—without requiring hardware changes. It reduces algorithmic inefficiency by using radiance warping, a technique that reuses previously computed lighting information rather than recalculating it, cutting the neural network's workload. It eliminates architectural inefficiency through two strategies: reorganizing memory access patterns to eliminate irregular, scattered trips to main memory (DRAM), and arranging data in the GPU's fast on-chip cache (SRAM) to prevent bank conflicts where simultaneous requests collide. Together, these interconnected fixes address both the algorithmic work required and how the mobile GPU hardware handles that work.
key_novelty: The key insight is solving both algorithmic bottlenecks in neural rendering (excessive computation and scattered memory access) and architectural bottlenecks in mobile GPUs (SRAM conflicts) together through software optimization, rather than treating them as separate problems.
contributions: Algorithm reducing computational work in NeRF model execution
Algorithm eliminating irregular DRAM accesses in rendering pipeline
On-chip data layout strategy eliminating SRAM bank conflicts
8.0x speedup and 7.9x energy savings on mobile Volta GPU with <1 dB PSNR loss
